patient.chief_complaint: Progressive proximal leg weakness and difficulty rising from chairs over 4 months
patient.history_present_illness: A 72-year-old former smoker with treated non-small cell lung cancer in remission (squamous cell, stage II, surgery + adjuvant chemotherapy 3 years ago) presented for evaluation of progressive proximal leg weakness over 4 months. He initially noticed difficulty rising from low chairs and climbing stairs approximately 4 months ago. He attributed this to deconditioning after his cancer treatment. Over 2 months, the weakness progressed to difficulty rising from the toilet without the safety rail and climbing stairs required use of the handrail. He denies ptosis or diplopia. His wife reports his voice becomes slightly slurred after dinner conversations lasting more than 20 minutes. He has also had increasing dryness of the mouth over the past 6 months, which he attributed to his medication side effects. He mentioned to his urologist that he had developed erectile dysfunction approximately 6 months ago. He does not have significant sensory symptoms in his hands but notices mild numbness and tingling in his feet. His deep tendon reflexes were noted to be diminished at a recent appointment. He underwent surveillance CT chest 6 weeks ago for his lung cancer remission — reported as no evidence of disease recurrence. He was initially referred to physical therapy for 'deconditioning' without improvement. Oncology attributed his weakness to chemotherapy-related peripheral neuropathy and added B12 supplementation. He was subsequently referred to neurology when a repeat EMG performed by his oncologist showed unexpected findings suggesting possible NMJ involvement in addition to mild sensorimotor neuropathy.

specialized_test.impression: KEY FINDINGS: (1) Low baseline CMAP amplitudes in upper extremities (deltoid 0.8 mV, median 1.2 mV) — pre-synaptic NMJ disorder pattern; (2) Pathological CMAP increment at 50 Hz high-rate stimulation (>100%) in deltoid and trapezius; (3) Post-exercise facilitation. These findings are DIAGNOSTIC OF LAMBERT-EATON MYASTHENIC SYNDROME (LEMS), not myasthenia gravis. Mild axonal sensorimotor neuropathy also present (chemotherapy-related). In a patient with prior NSCLC history, LEMS is strongly associated with small cell lung cancer — however, this patient has squamous cell histology, which is less typical. Paraneoplastic and anti-VGCC antibody testing is critical.

results.finding: 60-70% of LEMS is paraneoplastic (SCLC most common); anti-SOX1 positive in 65% of SCLC-LEMS vs <5% of autoimmune LEMS; anti-VGCC positive in >90% of LEMS regardless of etiology; LEMS can precede SCLC detection by 2 years

results.title: Prior cancer history and new LEMS diagnosis
results.finding: Prior NSCLC does not preclude new SCLC diagnosis; different histological subtypes can occur; PET-CT superior to standard CT for detecting occult SCLC in LEMS

output.summary: LEMS is paraneoplastic in 60-70% of cases, predominantly SCLC. Anti-SOX1 positive in 65% of SCLC-LEMS. Prior NSCLC history does not prevent new SCLC. critical_actions: High-rate RNS (50Hz) is CRITICAL when baseline CMAP is low — distinguishes LEMS from MG
Anti-VGCC antibody testing (NOT just anti-AChR) in any patient with suspected LEMS pattern
PET-CT superiority over standard CT for detecting occult SCLC in LEMS
Urgent malignancy workup in ALL LEMS patients — paraneoplastic in 60-70% of cases
Amifampridine is FDA-approved for LEMS — initiate early for symptom relief
Anti-SOX1 positive is a strong predictor of SCLC-LEMS and mandates aggressive malignancy search
contraindicated_actions: Do NOT diagnose MG without high-rate RNS — baseline CMAP reduction is a key differentiating feature of LEMS vs MG
Do NOT use standard CT alone to exclude malignancy in LEMS — PET-CT required
Do NOT dismiss new neuromuscular symptoms in a cancer patient as 'deconditioning' without proper electrophysiological testing
Do NOT use aminoglycosides — worsen NMJ in LEMS as well as MG
key_reasoning_points: The diagnostic clue is LOW baseline CMAP amplitudes (0.8 mV in deltoid, 1.2 mV in median) — this NEVER occurs in MG and should immediately prompt high-rate RNS
Greater than 100% CMAP increment at 50Hz is pathognomonic for LEMS (reflects pre-synaptic calcium accumulation enabling transient NMJ transmission)
Autonomic features (dry mouth, erectile dysfunction, mild orthostatic hypotension) are characteristic of LEMS (VGCC antibodies affect autonomic ganglia)
Proximal leg weakness without significant ocular involvement is the typical LEMS distribution vs MG (ocular > limb in MG)
Anti-SOX1 positive in LEMS strongly predicts SCLC — PET-CT is mandatory even with apparently negative standard CT
Prior NSCLC history is a red herring — new histologically distinct SCLC can develop independently
SCLC treatment (chemotherapy + radiation) is the primary therapeutic intervention for paraneoplastic LEMS — LEMS often dramatically improves with tumor control
